Last month, I was impacted by a company-wide layoff.

Once the initial shock wore off, I gave myself time to step back, reflect, and process everything. Here are three things this experience has taught me:

1. Your job is what you do, not who you are.
It’s easy to attach your entire identity and self-worth to a company or a title. But layoffs are business decisions, not personal reflections of your capabilities.

2. Your network is everything—nurture it before you need it.
The outpouring of support from former managers, peers, and mentors has been overwhelming in the best way. The relationships you build along the way are what truly endure.

3. Disruption creates clarity.
Being forced to pause gave me the space to ask: What do I actually enjoy doing? What kind of problems do I want to solve next? Sometimes the unexpected pivot is the push you needed.

To anyone else navigating a transition right now: be kind to yourself. It’s a marathon, not a sprint.

Most companies think remote work is about where people sit. 

It’s not. It’s about how work gets done.

The biggest mistake I see organizations make is taking an in-office culture and simply copy-pasting it onto Slack and Zoom:
- 8 hours of back-to-back video calls to "stay aligned"
- Constant pings expecting immediate responses
- Measuring presence and green dots instead of actual output

That’s not remote work; that’s remote micromanagement. And it burns people out fast.

The teams that actually thrive remotely do three things differently:
1. They default to asynchronous communication. Documentation over meetings. Clear briefs over quick calls.
2. They give people autonomy. If you hire smart people, let them manage their own time.
3. They evaluate results, not hours logged.

Remote work doesn’t break company culture—it exposes the flaws that were already there.

If you want remote to work, stop trying to recreate the office online. Redesign the way you work.

Early in my career, I made a mistake on a project that caused a major client escalation. 

I was terrified. I went into my 1-on-1 with my manager fully expecting a reprimand, maybe even to be taken off the account.

Instead, she closed her laptop, looked at me, and asked two questions:
1. "How can I help you fix it right now?"
2. "What do we need to put in place so this doesn't happen again?"

No blame. No anger. No public calling out. 

She backed me up in front of the client, helped me resolve the issue, and then sat down with me to review the process.

That day taught me what real leadership looks like. 

Weak leaders look for someone to blame when things go sideways. Great leaders take responsibility, protect their team, and turn failures into coaching moments.

Years later, whenever someone on my team makes a misstep, I remember that conversation. Culture isn't set by company values on a wall—it's set by how leaders react when things go wrong.

A lot of the conversation around AI in marketing focuses on doing things faster:
- 10x more blog posts
- Instant ad variations
- Automated email sequences

But volume was never marketing’s real bottleneck. Quality, relevance, and trust were.

Flooding channels with generic, AI-generated content isn't a strategy; it's noise. And buyers are getting remarkably good at tuning it out.

The real shift happening right now isn't about replacing human creativity. It’s about elevating it:
- Using AI to analyze complex customer data and uncover non-obvious insights in minutes.
- Automating repetitive tasks so strategists can spend more time actually talking to customers.
- Hyper-personalizing experiences at scale without losing brand voice.

AI raises the floor for everyone. Anyone can produce baseline content now.

Which means the premium on originality, deep domain expertise, authentic storytelling, and human connection just went way up.

Don't use AI to say more. Use it to understand your audience better so you can say something that actually matters.

5 things I wish someone had told me when I started out as a junior developer:

1. Asking questions early saves hours of frustration.
Struggling for 30–45 minutes is learning. Struggling in silence for 4 hours because you're afraid to look dumb is just stalling. Your seniors expect you to ask questions.

2. Code is read far more often than it is written.
Don't write clever, obscure one-liners to prove how smart you are. Write clear, readable, maintainable code that someone else (or future you) can easily debug at 2 AM.

3. Learn Git properly.
Understanding branching, rebasing, and how to read a commit history will save you from accidental panic attacks. Clean commits make you a joy to collaborate with.

4. Domain knowledge matters just as much as syntax.
Understanding the business problem you're solving makes you ten times more valuable than someone who just writes functions without understanding the "why."

5. You will never know everything, and that’s completely fine.
Tech moves fast. Being a great developer isn't about memorizing every framework; it's about getting comfortable with not knowing and knowing how to find the answer.

Keep building, be curious, and don't let imposter syndrome hold you back.

Two years ago, I went all-in on my first startup. 

Last week, we officially closed the doors.

It's hard to write that. When you pour your savings, your weekends, and your identity into building something, watching it not work out stings.

So what happened?
- We built a great product, but we didn't validate the willingness to pay early enough.
- We spent too much time perfecting features instead of aggressively testing distribution channels.
- We confused positive user feedback with sustainable product-market fit.

I used to view startup failure as a badge of shame. Now, I see it as the most expensive, intensive masterclass I could have ever taken. I learned how to hire, sell, build from scratch, manage cash flow, and lead through uncertainty.

To my co-founders, investors, and early adopters: thank you for believing in the vision and backing us. 

I’m taking a couple of weeks to decompress, reset, and figure out what’s next. To anyone in the arena right now: keep your head up.

We talk a lot about productivity, KPIs, and grinding for the next milestone. 

We don't talk nearly enough about mental health at work.

Burnout doesn't usually happen overnight. It creeps in slowly:
- Dreading opening your inbox in the morning
- Feeling like you're constantly behind, no matter how much you get done
- Losing the energy and creativity that made you love your work in the first place

For a long time, hustle culture framed working through exhaustion as a badge of honor. But chronically running on empty isn't dedication—it's unsustainable.

High performance and well-being aren't opposites. In fact, you can't have one long-term without the other.

If you’re a leader:
• Encourage your team to truly disconnect on weekends and vacations.
• Normalize taking mental health days without needing an elaborate excuse.
• Model healthy boundaries yourself.

And if you’re feeling overwhelmed right now: give yourself permission to step back and breathe. Your job needs you, but not at the expense of your health.

Last week, my flight was canceled due to bad weather. 

The line at the rebooking counter had about 80 stressed, angry travelers. By the time I reached the agent, I expected someone defensive and frazzled.

Instead, she took a breath, looked me in the eye, and said: "I know this completely ruins your plans today. Let’s see what we can do to get you home as smoothly as possible."

In less than five minutes, she found an alternate route, handed me my boarding pass with a warm smile, and wished me safe travels.

That interaction stuck with me, and it reminded me of a fundamental business truth:

People don't just judge your product or service when things go right. They judge your character by how you handle things when they go wrong.

In business:
1. Empathy diffuses tension faster than policy.
2. Speed and clear communication build trust when systems fail.
3. Frontline employees are the true face of your brand—empower them to solve problems.

Customer service isn't a department; it's the ultimate differentiator.

Unpopular opinion: Hustle culture isn't a badge of honor. It’s often just poor prioritization disguised as ambition.

Working 70-hour weeks, wearing sleep deprivation like a medal, and bragging about never taking time off doesn't make you more effective. It just makes you tired, reactive, and prone to bad decisions.

Output is not linear with hours worked:
- Creativity requires downtime.
- Strategic clarity requires cognitive rest.
- Sustainable growth requires pacing.

The most impressive professionals I know don't brag about how exhausted they are. They obsess over leverage, protect their energy, say no to low-impact tasks, and consistently deliver high-quality work in 40 focused hours.

Work hard, absolutely. But don't sacrifice your health, relationships, and long-term stamina just to look busy. 

Sustainability beats burnout every single time.

This week, my newsletter officially crossed 10,000 subscribers. 🎉

When I published the first edition 18 months ago, 14 people opened it (and half of them were family members). 

Here are the 4 biggest lessons from the journey from 0 to 10k:

1. Consistency over virality.
I stopped chasing one-hit-wonder viral posts and focused on sending high-value insights every Tuesday morning without fail. Readers value predictability and reliability.

2. Pick a specific problem, not a broad topic.
Instead of writing "general business thoughts," I narrowed down to [specific niche/problem]. When you speak to everyone, you reach no one. When you solve a specific headache, people share your work.

3. Distribution is half the work.
Great content doesn't market itself. Repurposing key newsletter insights into bite-sized LinkedIn posts and Twitter threads drove 60%+ of my subscriber growth.

4. Treat subscribers like humans, not metrics.
I reply to almost every email response. That 1-on-1 engagement turned casual readers into vocal advocates.

To everyone who opens, reads, and shares the newsletter each week: thank you so much for your support. 

On to the next milestone!

Networking as an introvert can feel exhausting. 

Walking into a crowded room full of strangers exchanging business cards and making small talk was always my nightmare. 

Over the years, I realized you don't have to be the loudest person in the room to build a strong professional network. Here’s what works for introverts:

1. Focus on depth, not breadth.
You don't need 50 business cards. Aim to have 1 or 2 meaningful, 1-on-1 conversations. Quality connections always beat superficial acquaintances.

2. Ask questions and listen.
Introverts are naturally great listeners. Most people love talking about their projects, challenges, and passions. Ask thoughtful, open-ended questions and let them do the talking.

3. Connect asynchronously.
LinkedIn, thoughtful comments, and personalized emails are great ways to build rapport without the sensory overload of networking mixers.

4. Follow up promptly.
The real relationship starts after the event. A simple, personalized message referencing something specific you discussed goes a long way.

Play to your strengths. Empathy, curiosity, and genuine listening are your superpowers.

When I first started in sales, I thought it was all about persuasion, pitches, and closing deals.

Years later, I’ve realized that working in sales didn’t just teach me how to sell—it taught me how to live.

A few lessons sales taught me about life:

1. Rejection is rarely personal.
A "no" usually just means bad timing, misaligned priorities, or lack of budget. In life and business, learning not to take rejection personally frees you to keep showing up.

2. Listening is ten times more powerful than talking.
The worst salespeople never stop talking. The best ones ask great questions and listen intently. People want to feel heard and understood—in negotiations, friendships, and relationships.

3. You can't control the outcome, only the inputs.
You can't force someone to buy. You can only control your preparation, your effort, and your follow-up. Focus on the process, and the results will follow.

4. Trust takes months to build and seconds to lose.
Never sacrifice your integrity for a short-term win.

Sales is fundamentally about understanding human nature. Once you understand that, everything changes.

Parenthood turns you into an absolute master of time management. You learn to cut through the noise and prioritize what truly moves the needle.

Why every Product Manager should learn SQL:

Early in my PM career, every data question required a ticket to the analytics team:
- "How many users dropped off at step 3?"
- "What’s the retention cohort for last month's feature launch?"
- "Which user segment uses this tool the most?"

Then I’d wait 3 to 5 days for an answer.

Once I learned basic SQL, everything changed:

1. Faster decision velocity.
Instead of waiting days for an analyst, you can query the database, validate a hypothesis, and unblock your engineering team in 15 minutes.

2. Better questions.
When you understand the data schema and how tables relate, your conversations with data scientists and engineers become much more nuanced and strategic.

3. Spotting hidden patterns.
Sometimes the most interesting product insights aren't on the standard dashboard. Writing your own queries lets you explore edge cases and anomalies firsthand.

You don't need to be a database architect. Basic SELECT, JOIN, GROUP BY, and WHERE clauses will give you 80% of what you need.

Data fluency is a product superpower.

A few years ago, I felt like my workday was entirely dictated by notifications: Slack pings, emails, meetings, and endless task switching. 

I was working 10 hours a day, but at the end of the week, I felt like I hadn’t accomplished anything meaningful.

Then I read "Deep Work" by Cal Newport. It completely shifted how I think about focus and productivity.

The core premise: the ability to perform deep, distraction-free work on cognitively demanding tasks is becoming increasingly rare—and therefore increasingly valuable.

Three changes I implemented after reading it:
1. Time-blocking non-negotiable focus blocks.
I block 2 hours every morning for high-priority creative/strategic work. Slack and email are completely closed.

2. Treating attention as a finite resource.
Context switching has a heavy cognitive tax. Grouping meetings into specific days or afternoons freed up uninterrupted mental space.

3. Embracing boredom.
Constantly reaching for your phone during micro-breaks ruins your capacity for sustained focus. Rest needs to be actual rest.

If you feel constantly busy but rarely productive, I can’t recommend this book enough. 

What book has had the biggest impact on your work habits?

This month marks 10 years since I put on my scrubs for my very first shift as a registered nurse.

A decade at the bedside teaches you things no textbook ever could:

1. Healing is more than medicine.
Administering treatments and monitoring vitals is the technical job. But holding a frightened patient’s hand, truly listening, and explaining things with kindness is often what makes the biggest difference.

2. People show you who they are in their most vulnerable moments.
Illness strips away pretense. I've witnessed incredible resilience, unconditional love from families, and quiet courage in the face of heartbreak.

3. Teamwork is literally lifesaving.
Healthcare isn't an individual sport. The bond you build with fellow nurses, doctors, techs, and support staff during a chaotic 12-hour shift is unlike anything else.

4. You can't pour from an empty cup.
In a field dedicated to caring for others, learning to set boundaries and protect your own physical and mental well-being is essential for longevity.

It hasn't always been easy—there were shifts that pushed me to my absolute limits. But having the privilege to care for people on their hardest days has been the honor of my life.

Here's to the next chapter. 🩺💙

Recruiter confession:

The biggest mistake I see candidates make in interviews isn't a resume gap, a nervous stutter, or not knowing every technical answer.

It's failing to connect their experience to the specific business impact.

Too many candidates answer questions by listing their daily tasks:
- "I managed our social media accounts."
- "I wrote code for the backend API."
- "I ran weekly team standups."

While that explains what you did, it doesn't tell the interviewer *why it mattered*.

Strong candidates frame their answers around impact:
- What problem were you solving?
- What was the measurable outcome? (Did you increase revenue? Cut latency? Save the team 5 hours a week?)
- What did you learn along the way?

Companies don't just hire people to perform tasks; they hire people to solve problems and drive results.

In your next interview, shift from "here's what I did" to "here's the impact I made." It makes a world of difference.

A year ago, I made one of the scariest decisions of my life: I left my career as a high school teacher to become a UX Designer.

At first, imposter syndrome was real. I worried that years in the classroom wouldn't translate to the tech world.

I was wrong. 

Teaching and UX design are surprisingly similar:
- Empathy: Understanding diverse student learning styles is identical to understanding user personas and pain points.
- Information Architecture: Breaking down complex concepts into engaging, digestible lesson plans is essentially designing intuitive user journeys.
- Iteration & Feedback: Adjusting curriculum based on student engagement is rapid user testing in real time.

If you’re thinking about making a career transition: don’t discount your non-traditional background. The technical tools (Figma, design systems) can be learned. But empathy, communication, and human-centered problem solving? That’s your competitive edge.

So excited to continue growing in this field!

One of the most underrated career skills is learning how to say "no."

Early in our careers, we're taught to say yes to everything:
- Yes to every project
- Yes to every meeting invite
- Yes to every favor, request, and committee

We think saying yes makes us helpful, ambitious, and indispensable.

In reality, saying yes to everything means saying no to your core priorities, your focus, and your well-being. It leads to shallow work, missed deadlines, and eventual burnout.

Saying "no" isn't about being uncooperative. It's about protecting your capacity to do exceptional work on what truly matters.

How to say no professionally:
- "I’d love to help, but with my current commitments to [Project X], I won’t be able to give this the attention it deserves."
- "If I take this on, which of our existing priorities should I deprioritize?"
- "I can't take the lead on this, but I'm happy to review the final draft for 15 minutes."

Focus is defined by what you choose NOT to do.

One year ago, I left my full-time agency job to go all-in as a freelance designer.

It has been one of the most rewarding—and humbling—years of my professional life.

Here are 4 lessons I learned the hard way:

1. You aren't just a designer anymore.
You are also sales, accounting, project management, and customer support. If you don't enjoy running a business, freelancing will feel exhausting.

2. Contracts and deposits are non-negotiable.
Never start work without a signed contract and an upfront deposit. Clear scope protects both you and the client.

3. Cash flow management beats raw income.
A $10k month feels amazing until you realize next month might be $2k. Build a 6-month buffer and smooth out your income so you never take bad projects out of desperation.

4. Referrals are your best pipeline.
Over 80% of my work came from former colleagues, existing clients, and word-of-mouth. Deliver great work, communicate proactively, and people will happily recommend you.

To every client, mentor, and fellow freelancer who supported me this year: thank you. Year two, let's go!
